mcqs.question: What is a distinguishing risk of a tmux/tmate-based remote pairing session compared to a browser-based coding environment?
options: It requires no local setup at all, unlike a browser IDE
A connection drop can lose all session context unless it's inside a persistent multiplexer
It cannot be used for any language other than shell scripting
It always runs faster than a browser-based environment regardless of connection quality
mcqs.explanation: Terminal multiplexer sharing is prone to losing context entirely on a dropped connection unless the session persists independently — that's its distinct failure mode. It does require some setup, works with any language run in the terminal, and speed depends on connection quality, not the tool category.

mcqs.question: You're told the interview will use a specific IDE collaboration extension you've never used before. What's the best move?
options: Wait until the interview starts and learn it live, since it's untimed anyway
Assume any similar extension you already know will behave the same way
Install and test that exact extension before the interview so it isn't your first time using it during a scored round
Ask the interviewer to switch to a tool you already know instead
mcqs.explanation: Testing the named tool beforehand removes an avoidable source of friction; the first time using any tool should never be during the scored round itself. It generally isn't untimed, similar tools can differ in meaningful ways, and asking to swap the interviewer's chosen tool isn't a reasonable first move.

mcqs.question: Why does narrating actions before taking them matter more in remote pairing than in-person pairing?
options: It's mainly a formality expected regardless of format
The remote partner can't infer intent from body language, so narration is the only substitute
It's required by most remote-pairing tools' terms of use
Remote sessions are always recorded, so narration creates a verbal record
mcqs.explanation: Remote pairing removes the in-person cues a partner would normally use to infer intent, making verbal narration the substitute channel for that information. It isn't a formality, isn't a tooling requirement, and recording (where it happens) isn't the reason narration matters.

mcqs.question: You notice your typing appears delayed on the shared screen during a pairing round. What should you do?
options: Say so immediately and confirm whether the other person is seeing the delay too
Keep working normally and hope the lag resolves on its own
Stop typing entirely until the interviewer mentions it first
Restart your machine without telling the interviewer what's happening
mcqs.explanation: Flagging lag immediately lets both people adjust and confirms whether it's actually affecting the shared view. Silently continuing or freezing wastes time hoping it resolves, and restarting without communicating leaves your partner confused about what just happened.

mcqs.question: You spot an obvious small fix in a shared remote-pairing session. Why is silently typing it, even though it's correct, a mistake?
options: It's technically against the rules of most pairing-tool licenses
It will always introduce a bug even if the fix looks correct
It makes the shared session lag more than typing with narration would
It leaves the partner watching a cursor move with no idea why, undercutting the collaboration signal being tested
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is that remote pairing relies on narration as the partner's only window into your reasoning — silent action, even correct action, removes that entirely and reads as working alone with an audience. It has nothing to do with licensing, bug likelihood, or lag.
